notes:
1. Meaning of a Union Territory

  • A Union Territory is a constitutional territorial unit administered principally by the Union government.
  • Union Territories are governed mainly under Part VIII of the Constitution.
  • Unlike States, Union Territories do not occupy the same position as constituent units in the federal distribution of powers.
  • They are normally administered by the President through an Administrator appointed by the President.
  • Union Territories form part of the territory of India under Article 1.
📌 Must-Memorise

Union Territory → Part VIII → Principally Administered by Union

2. Why Union Territories Were Created

Union Territory status has been used for territories requiring greater or more direct Union administration because of factors such as:

  • Small geographical size.
  • Limited population.
  • Strategic location.
  • National-capital requirements.
  • Cultural and historical distinctiveness.
  • Administrative convenience.
  • Political transition before Statehood.
  • Border and security considerations.

3. Different Models of Union Territory Administration

  • All Union Territories do not follow one identical constitutional model.

A Union Territory may be:

  • Directly administered without a Legislature.
  • Provided with a Legislative Assembly.
  • Provided with a Council of Ministers.
  • Governed through special constitutional provisions.
  • Governed through a parliamentary statute.
  • This creates constitutional asymmetry even among Union Territories themselves.
📌 TNPSC Key Concept

All Union Territories → Not Governed Identically

4. Union Territories Are Not Local Bodies

  • A Union Territory is a constitutional territorial unit.

It should not be confused with:

  • District administration.
  • Municipal Corporation.
  • Municipality.
  • Panchayat.
  • Ordinary Union government department.
  • Its constitutional position arises from the Constitution, parliamentary laws, reorganisation laws and special provisions.

5. Part VIII — The Union Territories

  • Part VIII of the Constitution is titled “The Union Territories.”

Its principal provisions include:

  • Article 239.
  • Article 239A.
  • Article 239AA.
  • Article 239AB.
  • Article 239B.
  • Article 240.
  • Article 241.
  • Article 242 originally related to Coorg but was repealed after territorial reorganisation.
📌 Must-Memorise

Part VIII → Union Territories
Articles → 239–241 with inserted Articles 239A–239B

6. Constitutional Position of Union Territories

  • Union Territories form part of the territory of India under Article 1.
  • They are not generally governed through Part VI, which applies to States.

Their administration primarily operates through:

  • Part VIII.
  • Parliamentary legislation.
  • Presidential regulations.
  • Reorganisation laws.
  • Special constitutional provisions.
  • Parliament retains greater constitutional authority over Union Territories than over ordinary State subjects.

7. State vs Union Territory

  • A State is a constituent unit of the Indian federal system.
  • A Union Territory is principally administered by the Union.
  • A Union Territory may possess a Legislature, Chief Minister and Council of Ministers.
  • Such institutions do not make it constitutionally identical to a State.
  • Parliament retains broader legislative and administrative power over Union Territories.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

UT with Legislature ≠ State

8. Present Union Territories of India

India presently has eight Union Territories:

  • Andaman and Nicobar Islands.
  • Chandigarh.
  • Dadra and Nagar Haveli and Daman and Diu.
  • National Capital Territory of Delhi.
  • Jammu and Kashmir.
  • Ladakh.
  • Lakshadweep.
  • Puducherry.
📌 Must-Memorise

Present Union Territories → 8

9. Union Territories with Legislatures

The Union Territories with legislative frameworks are:

  • National Capital Territory of Delhi.
  • Puducherry.
  • Jammu and Kashmir.
  • Their Legislatures do not possess identical powers.
  • Each operates under a different constitutional or statutory framework.
📌 Must-Memorise

UTs with Legislatures → Delhi + Puducherry + Jammu and Kashmir

10. Union Territories without Legislative Assemblies

The Union Territories without Legislative Assemblies are:

  • Andaman and Nicobar Islands.
  • Chandigarh.
  • Dadra and Nagar Haveli and Daman and Diu.
  • Ladakh.
  • Lakshadweep.

11. Article 239 — General Administration

  • Article 239 provides the general constitutional rule for administration of Union Territories.
  • Every Union Territory is administered by the President unless Parliament provides otherwise by law.
  • The President acts through an Administrator.
  • The Administrator is appointed by the President.
  • The President specifies the designation of the Administrator.
📌 Must-Memorise

Article 239 → Administration of Union Territories by President

12. Administrator as Representative of the President

  • The Administrator functions as the representative of the President.
  • The Administrator is not constitutionally identical to a Governor of a State.

Presidential authority may determine:

  • Designation.
  • Delegated powers.
  • Administrative responsibilities.
  • Rules of business.
  • In the parliamentary system, presidential functions are ordinarily exercised on the aid and advice of the Union Council of Ministers.

13. Governor of a State as Administrator of a UT

  • The President may appoint the Governor of a neighbouring State as Administrator of a Union Territory.
  • When acting as Administrator, the Governor performs a separate constitutional role.
  • In that capacity, the Governor does not act on the advice of the State Council of Ministers.
  • The offices of State Governor and Union Territory Administrator remain legally distinct.
⚠️ TNPSC Favourite

Same Person → Governor + UT Administrator Possible
Roles → Constitutionally Separate

14. Governor vs Administrator

Governor of a State:

  • Functions under Part VI.
  • Constitutional head of a State.
  • Ordinarily acts on advice of State Council of Ministers.

Administrator of Union Territory:

  • Functions under Article 239.
  • Represents the President.
  • Operates within Union Territory framework.
  • Subject to Union constitutional and statutory control.

15. Administrator, Lieutenant Governor and Chief Commissioner

  • “Administrator” is the general constitutional expression used in Article 239.
  • The President may give the office different designations.

Common designations include:

  • Lieutenant Governor.
  • Administrator.
  • Chief Commissioner.
  • The designation depends on the Union Territory and applicable constitutional or statutory arrangement.

16. Lieutenant Governors

Lieutenant Governors commonly administer larger or specially structured Union Territories such as:

  • Delhi.
  • Puducherry.
  • Jammu and Kashmir.
  • Ladakh.
  • Andaman and Nicobar Islands may also be administered through a Lieutenant Governor under the applicable designation.
  • The exact designation is determined through law or presidential notification.

17. Administrators

Administrators may be appointed for Union Territories such as:

  • Chandigarh.
  • Lakshadweep.
  • Dadra and Nagar Haveli and Daman and Diu.
  • The Administrator is appointed, not elected.

18. Administrator Is Not an Elected Office

  • An Administrator or Lieutenant Governor is appointed by the President.
  • The office is not directly elected by the people.
  • It is not politically responsible to the territorial Legislature in the same manner as a Chief Minister.
  • Where a Legislature exists, relations between the Administrator and ministers depend on the specific constitutional or statutory framework.

19. Parliament's Legislative Power over Union Territories

  • Parliament possesses extensive power to legislate for Union Territories.

Parliament may legislate on:

  • Union List.
  • State List.
  • Concurrent List

for Union Territories.

  • This is a major distinction between States and Union Territories.
📌 Must-Memorise

Parliament + UT → Can Legislate on All Three Lists

20. Why Parliament Can Legislate on State List for UTs

  • The State List primarily limits Parliament's ordinary power in relation to States.
  • Union Territories do not occupy the same federal legislative position as States.
  • Therefore Parliament retains broader legislative competence over Union Territories.
📌 TNPSC Key Concept

State → Greater Constitutional Autonomy
UT → Broader Parliamentary Control

21. Local Legislature Does Not Eliminate Parliament's Power

  • Even where a Union Territory has a Legislative Assembly, Parliament retains legislative power over that territory.
  • The local Legislature's power is therefore not exclusive.
  • Parliamentary law may prevail according to the applicable constitutional framework.
  • This distinguishes Union Territory self-government from State autonomy.

22. Union Territories without Legislature

A Union Territory without a Legislature is principally administered through:

  • President.
  • Administrator or Lieutenant Governor.
  • Union ministries.
  • Territorial administrative departments.
  • Parliament performs the legislative role.

23. Union Territories with Legislature

A Legislature may exist through:

  • A constitutional provision.
  • A parliamentary statute.
  • A reorganisation law.

Present models include:

  • Delhi.
  • Puducherry.
  • Jammu and Kashmir.
  • Their powers are not identical.

24. Difference among Legislative Union Territories

Delhi, Puducherry and Jammu and Kashmir differ in:

  • Constitutional basis.
  • Excluded legislative subjects.
  • Administrator's powers.
  • Parliamentary control.
  • Service arrangements.
  • Composition and structure of Legislature.
  • Statutory framework.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

Delhi = Puducherry = J&K in Powers? → No

25. Article 239A

  • Article 239A was inserted by the Fourteenth Constitutional Amendment Act, 1962.

It authorised Parliament to create:

  • A Legislature.
  • A Council of Ministers.
  • Or both

for certain Union Territories.

  • It is now principally associated with Puducherry.
📌 Must-Memorise

Article 239A → Puducherry Model
14th Amendment, 1962 → Inserted Article 239A

26. Government of Union Territories Act, 1963

  • Parliament enacted the Government of Union Territories Act, 1963.

It provides for matters such as:

  • Legislative Assemblies.
  • Councils of Ministers.
  • Legislative procedure.
  • Financial administration.
  • Relations between Administrator and ministers.
  • It forms the major statutory basis for Puducherry's territorial government.

27. Puducherry Legislative Structure

Puducherry has:

  • Elected Legislative Assembly.
  • Council of Ministers.
  • Chief Minister.
  • Lieutenant Governor.
  • Its Legislature operates within the framework of Article 239A and the Government of Union Territories Act, 1963.

28. Nominated Members in Puducherry

  • The statutory framework permits nominated membership in the Puducherry Legislative Assembly.
  • This is an important distinction from an ordinary State Legislative Assembly.
  • Puducherry therefore has a distinctive Union Territory legislative arrangement.
📌 TNPSC Key Point

Puducherry Assembly → Nominated Membership Permitted under Statutory Framework

29. Puducherry Legislature's Competence

The Puducherry Legislature may legislate on permitted subjects in:

  • State List.
  • Concurrent List.

Its power remains subject to:

  • Parliamentary supremacy.
  • Constitutional limitations.
  • Statutory provisions.
  • Administrator and presidential arrangements.
  • Parliament retains authority to legislate for Puducherry even in areas within the territorial Legislature's field.

30. Article 239AA — Delhi

  • Article 239AA was inserted by the Sixty-Ninth Constitutional Amendment Act, 1991.
  • Delhi was redesignated as the National Capital Territory of Delhi.
  • Its Administrator was designated as the Lieutenant Governor.
  • Article 239AA created a special constitutional model for Delhi.
📌 Must-Memorise

69th Amendment, 1991 → Article 239AA → NCT of Delhi

31. Why Delhi Has a Special Constitutional Model

Delhi is:

  • National capital.
  • Seat of Union government.
  • Location of Parliament.
  • Location of Supreme Court.
  • Centre of foreign diplomatic activity.
  • Major urban population centre.
  • The Constitution therefore combines elected territorial government with strong Union control over specified matters.

32. Institutions under Article 239AA

Delhi has:

  • Legislative Assembly.
  • Council of Ministers.
  • Chief Minister.
  • Lieutenant Governor.
  • Despite these institutions, Delhi remains a Union Territory and is not a full State.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

NCT of Delhi → Union Territory
Not Full State

33. Government of NCT of Delhi Act, 1991

  • The Government of National Capital Territory of Delhi Act, 1991 supplements Article 239AA.

It provides institutional and procedural rules for:

  • Legislative Assembly.
  • Council of Ministers.
  • Administration.
  • Legislative functioning.
  • Delhi's constitutional arrangement therefore rests on both constitutional and statutory provisions.

34. Legislative Powers of Delhi Assembly

  • Delhi Legislative Assembly may legislate on permitted subjects in the State List and Concurrent List insofar as they apply to Union Territories.
  • Its legislative power is constitutionally limited.
  • Parliament retains broader legislative competence over Delhi.

35. Subjects Excluded from Delhi Assembly

Delhi Assembly cannot ordinarily legislate on:

  • Public Order.
  • Police.
  • Land.

These correspond primarily to State List Entries:

  • Entry 1.
  • Entry 2.
  • Entry 18.
  • Connected entries specified by the Constitution are also excluded.
📌 Must-Memorise

Delhi Excluded Subjects → Public Order + Police + Land

36. Parliament's Power over Delhi

Parliament can legislate for Delhi on:

  • Union List.
  • State List.
  • Concurrent List.
  • Parliamentary legislative competence is therefore wider than that of the Delhi Assembly.
  • Delhi's Legislature does not possess exclusive State-like legislative authority.

37. Conflict between Parliamentary and Delhi Laws

  • Where a Delhi law conflicts with parliamentary law, parliamentary law generally prevails.
  • A Delhi law reserved for and receiving presidential assent may operate in specified circumstances.
  • Parliament nevertheless retains power to later override such territorial legislation.

38. Lieutenant Governor of Delhi

  • The Lieutenant Governor is the Administrator of the National Capital Territory.
  • The office creates a constitutional link between the Union and Delhi territorial government.
  • The Lieutenant Governor's constitutional position is distinct from that of a State Governor.
  • Delhi's special constitutional framework gives the Union a more direct role.

39. Delhi Council of Ministers

  • Delhi has a Council of Ministers headed by the Chief Minister.
  • It aids and advises the Lieutenant Governor on matters within the Assembly's legislative competence, subject to constitutional exceptions.
  • The Chief Minister is appointed by the President.
  • Other ministers are appointed within the constitutional and statutory framework.

40. Difference of Opinion in Delhi

  • Article 239AA provides a mechanism where disagreement arises between the Lieutenant Governor and ministers.
  • Specified differences may be referred to the President.
  • Urgent interim action may be taken in circumstances permitted by the constitutional framework.
  • Constitutional cooperation and responsible government remain important principles.

41. Delhi Lieutenant Governor vs State Governor

Delhi Lieutenant Governor:

  • Administrator of a Union Territory.
  • Parliament has broader legislative power.
  • Public order, police and land remain outside local legislative control.
  • Constitution permits reference of certain disagreements to President.

State Governor:

  • Constitutional head under Part VI.
  • Functions within State's federal constitutional status.
  • State Legislature has constitutionally assigned State List powers.

42. Article 239AB — Failure of Constitutional Machinery in Delhi

  • Article 239AB applies specifically to the National Capital Territory of Delhi.

It may operate where administration cannot be carried on according to:

  • Article 239AA.
  • Government of NCT of Delhi Act.
  • It may also operate where presidential action is considered necessary for proper administration.
📌 Must-Memorise

Article 239AB → Failure of Constitutional Machinery in Delhi

43. Consequences under Article 239AB

  • The President may suspend operation of specified provisions of Article 239AA.
  • Related statutory provisions may also be suspended to the extent constitutionally permitted.
  • The elected territorial governmental framework may therefore be suspended or modified.
  • Administration may then operate under presidential authority.

44. Article 239AB vs Article 356

Article 356:

  • Applies to States.
  • Deals with failure of constitutional machinery in a State.

Article 239AB:

  • Applies specifically to Delhi.
  • Operates under Delhi's special Union Territory constitutional framework.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

Delhi → Article 239AB
Not Article 356 Directly

45. Article 239B — Ordinance-Making Power

  • Article 239B permits the Administrator of a Union Territory having a Legislature to promulgate an Ordinance in specified circumstances.
  • The Legislature must not be in session.
  • Immediate action must be considered necessary.
  • Presidential instructions are required before promulgation.
📌 Must-Memorise

Article 239B → Administrator's Ordinance Power

46. Presidential Instructions for Ordinance

  • The Administrator cannot promulgate an Ordinance under Article 239B without instructions from the President.
  • This highlights continuing Union control over territorial legislative administration.

47. Force and Limits of Ordinance

  • An Ordinance has the same force and effect as an Act of the territorial Legislature.

It remains subject to:

  • Constitutional limits.
  • Parliamentary authority.
  • Legislative approval requirements.
  • An Ordinance cannot contain provisions that the territorial Legislature itself lacks power to enact.

48. Withdrawal and Duration of Ordinance

  • An Ordinance must be placed before the Legislature.
  • It ceases to operate after the constitutionally or statutorily prescribed period unless approved.
  • It may be withdrawn by the Administrator with presidential instructions.

49. Article 239B and Puducherry

  • Article 239B is particularly relevant to Puducherry's legislative framework.
  • Delhi's Ordinance arrangements operate through its own special constitutional and statutory structure and are not identical in every respect.

50. Article 240 — Presidential Regulations

  • Article 240 empowers the President to make regulations for the peace, progress and good government of specified Union Territories.
  • This provides a direct legislative mechanism for certain Union Territories without full local legislative institutions.
📌 Must-Memorise

Article 240 → President → Peace, Progress and Good Government

51. Union Territories Relevant to Article 240

The current principal non-legislative Union Territories connected with Article 240 include:

  • Andaman and Nicobar Islands.
  • Lakshadweep.
  • Dadra and Nagar Haveli and Daman and Diu.
  • Application depends on the precise constitutional text and territorial legislative status.

52. Force of Presidential Regulation

A regulation under Article 240 may:

  • Have the same force as an Act of Parliament.
  • Amend a parliamentary law applicable to that Union Territory.
  • Repeal a parliamentary law applicable there.
  • Amend or repeal existing local law.
⚠️ TNPSC Favourite

Article 240 Regulation → Can Have Force of Act of Parliament

53. Article 240 and Legislative Union Territories

  • Where a Union Territory has a functioning Legislature, the President's regulation-making power may be restricted or suspended according to the constitutional provision.
  • Such power may revive in circumstances such as dissolution or suspension of the Legislature where permitted.

54. Presidential Regulation vs Executive Order

Presidential Regulation:

  • Legislative character.
  • Can have force of parliamentary law.

Executive Order:

  • Administrative character.
  • Does not automatically possess equivalent legislative force.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

Article 240 Regulation ≠ Ordinary Executive Order

55. Article 241 — High Courts for Union Territories

  • Article 241 empowers Parliament in relation to High Courts for Union Territories.

Parliament may:

  • Constitute a High Court for a Union Territory.
  • Declare an existing court to be its High Court.
  • Extend a State High Court's jurisdiction.
  • Exclude or alter such jurisdiction according to law.
📌 Must-Memorise

Article 241 → High Courts for Union Territories

56. Different High Court Models for UTs

A Union Territory may:

  • Have its own High Court.
  • Share a High Court with a State.
  • Share a common High Court with another Union Territory.
  • Judicial arrangement does not determine Statehood.

57. Delhi High Court

  • Delhi has its own High Court.
  • The existence of its own High Court does not make Delhi a State.
  • Delhi continues to be a Union Territory with a special constitutional framework.

58. Common High Court for Jammu and Kashmir and Ladakh

  • Jammu and Kashmir and Ladakh share a common High Court under the Jammu and Kashmir Reorganisation framework.
  • The judicial arrangement serves both Union Territories.
  • Sharing a High Court does not alter their territorial status.

59. Jammu and Kashmir Reorganisation, 2019

  • The Jammu and Kashmir Reorganisation Act, 2019 reorganised the former State of Jammu and Kashmir.
  • The reorganisation took effect on 31 October 2019.

It created:

  • Union Territory of Jammu and Kashmir with a Legislature.
  • Union Territory of Ladakh without a Legislature.
📌 Must-Memorise

31 October 2019 → J&K Reorganisation
J&K → UT with Legislature
Ladakh → UT without Legislature

60. Territorial Composition of Ladakh

Ladakh comprises:

  • Leh.
  • Kargil.
  • It is administered through a Lieutenant Governor and Union administrative framework.
  • It has no Legislative Assembly.
📌 Must-Memorise

Ladakh → Leh + Kargil → No Legislature

61. Jammu and Kashmir Legislative Framework

Jammu and Kashmir has:

  • Lieutenant Governor.
  • Legislative Assembly.
  • Council of Ministers.
  • Legislative powers under the Jammu and Kashmir Reorganisation Act, 2019.
  • Its powers remain subject to statutory exclusions and Parliament's broader authority.

62. Jammu and Kashmir vs Ladakh

Jammu and Kashmir:

  • Union Territory.
  • Has Legislature.
  • Has provision for Council of Ministers.

Ladakh:

  • Union Territory.
  • No Legislature.
  • Direct Union administration through Lieutenant Governor.
⚠️ TNPSC Favourite

J&K → Legislature
Ladakh → No Legislature

63. Parliamentary Representation of Union Territories

  • Union Territories may receive representation in the Lok Sabha.

Representation depends on:

  • Constitutional provisions.
  • Parliamentary law.
  • Delimitation.
  • Territorial status.
  • Union Territories do not receive equal parliamentary representation.

64. Rajya Sabha Representation of UTs

  • Not every Union Territory is represented in Rajya Sabha.
  • Rajya Sabha representation exists only where constitutional and statutory arrangements provide for it.

Union Territories represented in Rajya Sabha include larger legislative territories such as:

  • Delhi.
  • Puducherry.
  • Jammu and Kashmir.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

Every UT Has Rajya Sabha Seats? → No

65. Fourth Schedule and UT Representation

  • Allocation of Rajya Sabha seats is contained in the Fourth Schedule.
  • Territorial status, population and statutory arrangements influence representation.
  • Union Territories do not receive equal numbers of Rajya Sabha seats.

66. Administrator Does Not Represent UT in Parliament

  • An Administrator or Lieutenant Governor does not become a voting parliamentary representative merely by holding administrative office.
  • Parliamentary representation arises through electoral and statutory mechanisms.

67. Territorial Classification in 1950

The original Constitution classified territorial units as:

  • Part A States.
  • Part B States.
  • Part C States.
  • Part D territory.
  • Several territories later treated as Union Territories had previously been Part C or Part D units.

68. Creation of Union Territory Category in 1956

  • The Seventh Constitutional Amendment and States Reorganisation Act, 1956 reorganised India's territorial structure.
  • They abolished the old Part A, B, C and D classification.
  • The modern constitutional category of Union Territories emerged through this reorganisation.
📌 Must-Memorise

1956 → Union Territory Category under Reorganised Structure

69. French Territories

Former French-controlled territories included:

  • Puducherry.
  • Karaikal.
  • Mahe.
  • Yanam.
  • Chandernagore.
  • Chandernagore later merged with West Bengal.
  • Puducherry, Karaikal, Mahe and Yanam became components of Puducherry.

70. Puducherry's Territorial Components

Puducherry consists of geographically separated former French settlements including:

  • Puducherry.
  • Karaikal.
  • Mahe.
  • Yanam.
⚠️ TNPSC Favourite

Puducherry UT → Puducherry + Karaikal + Mahe + Yanam

71. Portuguese Territories

Former Portuguese territories integrated into India included:

  • Goa.
  • Daman.
  • Diu.
  • Dadra and Nagar Haveli.
  • Goa later became a State.
  • Other territories continued under Union Territory arrangements before later reorganisation.

72. Union Territories That Became States

Examples include:

  • Himachal Pradesh.
  • Manipur.
  • Tripura.
  • Mizoram.
  • Arunachal Pradesh.
  • Goa.
  • Union Territory status has therefore sometimes acted as a transitional stage before Statehood.

73. Delhi's Special Status, 1991

  • The Sixty-Ninth Constitutional Amendment Act, 1991 created the modern National Capital Territory framework.
  • Article 239AA was inserted.
  • Delhi received a Legislative Assembly and Council of Ministers within a special Union Territory structure.
📌 Must-Memorise

69th Amendment → NCT Delhi

74. 2019 Territorial Changes

The former State of Jammu and Kashmir was reorganised into:

  • Jammu and Kashmir.
  • Ladakh.
  • Both became Union Territories.
  • Their constitutional models differ because only Jammu and Kashmir has a Legislature.

75. Merger of Dadra and Nagar Haveli and Daman and Diu

  • Dadra and Nagar Haveli and Daman and Diu were earlier separate Union Territories.
  • They were merged in 2020.

The new Union Territory is named:

  • Dadra and Nagar Haveli and Daman and Diu.
📌 Must-Memorise

2020 → DNH + Daman and Diu → One UT

76. States vs Union Territories — Constitutional Foundation

State:

  • Part VI.
  • Constituent unit of federal system.

Union Territory:

  • Part VIII.
  • Principally administered by Union.
📌 Must-Memorise

State → Part VI
UT → Part VIII

77. States vs Union Territories — Executive Head

State:

  • Governor.

Union Territory:

  • Administrator or Lieutenant Governor.
  • A Union Territory may additionally have a Chief Minister where a Legislature and Council of Ministers exist.

78. States vs Union Territories — Legislature

State:

  • Constitutionally provided State Legislature.

Union Territory:

  • Legislature exists only where Constitution or Parliament provides one.
📌 TNPSC Key Concept

State Legislature → Standard Constitutional Institution
UT Legislature → Special Arrangement

79. States vs Union Territories — Legislative Power

State:

  • Legislature possesses constitutionally assigned State List competence.

Union Territory:

  • Parliament has broad power over Union, State and Concurrent Lists.
  • Local Legislature, if present, has limited and non-exclusive powers.

80. States vs Union Territories — Parliamentary Control

State:

  • Parliament ordinarily cannot legislate on State List matters except under constitutional exceptions.

Union Territory:

  • Parliament can legislate even on State List subjects.
📌 Must-Memorise

UT → Wider Parliamentary Legislative Power

81. States vs Union Territories — Administrative Control

State:

  • Constitutionally autonomous within assigned sphere.

Union Territory:

  • Subject to greater direct Union administrative control.

82. States vs Union Territories — Rajya Sabha Representation

State:

  • All States receive representation in Rajya Sabha.

Union Territory:

  • Only specified Union Territories receive representation.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

All States → Rajya Sabha Representation
All UTs → No

83. Conversion of Territorial Status

  • Parliament may convert a Union Territory into a State.
  • Parliament may reorganise a State into one or more Union Territories.
  • Parliament may merge or divide territorial units.
  • Appropriate constitutional and statutory procedure must be followed.

84. New Delhi Municipal Council v. State of Punjab, 1997

  • The Supreme Court examined Delhi's constitutional character.
  • It reaffirmed that Delhi remains a Union Territory.
  • Delhi's special constitutional institutions do not make it a State.
  • Parliament retains broader constitutional authority over Delhi.
📌 Must-Memorise

NDMC v. State of Punjab, 1997 → Delhi Remains UT

85. Government of NCT of Delhi v. Union of India, 2018

  • A Constitution Bench considered the relationship between Delhi's elected government and Lieutenant Governor.

The Court emphasised:

  • Representative government.
  • Constitutional morality.
  • Collective responsibility.
  • Cooperative governance.
  • It emphasised that the Lieutenant Governor should not refer every routine disagreement to the President.
  • Delhi's special constitutional limitations nevertheless remain.
📌 Must-Memorise

GNCTD Case, 2018 → Representative Government + Constitutional Cooperation

86. Government of NCT of Delhi v. Union of India, 2023

  • The Supreme Court examined legislative and executive control over services in Delhi under the constitutional and statutory framework then in force.
  • Parliament subsequently amended the Government of NCT of Delhi Act in 2023.
  • Exact present service-control arrangements are an evolving legal and current-affairs area.

87. Enduring Delhi Exam Principles

For static TNPSC preparation, remember:

  • Delhi has representative government.
  • Delhi remains a Union Territory.
  • Parliament retains wider and overriding legislative powers.
  • Public order, police and land remain outside the Delhi Assembly's ordinary legislative competence.
  • Lieutenant Governor has a special constitutional position.
  • Delhi is not constitutionally identical to a State.

88. Important Article Mapping

  • Article 1 → Territory of India includes Union Territories.
  • Article 239 → Administration of Union Territories.
  • Article 239A → Legislature/Council of Ministers for specified UTs; principally Puducherry.
  • Article 239AA → Special provisions for Delhi.
  • Article 239AB → Failure of constitutional machinery in Delhi.
  • Article 239B → Ordinance power for Administrator of UT with Legislature.
  • Article 240 → Presidential regulations.
  • Article 241 → High Courts for Union Territories.

89. Amendment Mapping

  • 7th Amendment, 1956 → Territorial reorganisation and modern UT framework.
  • 14th Amendment, 1962 → Inserted Article 239A.
  • 69th Amendment, 1991 → Inserted Article 239AA and created NCT Delhi framework.
📌 Must-Memorise

7th → UT Framework
14th → 239A
69th → 239AA

90. TNPSC Traps

  • Union Territory → Constitutional territorial unit.
  • Union Territory ≠ Local body.
  • Part VIII → Union Territories.
  • Article 239 → President administers UTs.
  • Administrator → Appointed by President.
  • Administrator ≠ State Governor.
  • Governor may also serve as UT Administrator in separate capacity.
  • Administrator → Not elected.
  • Parliament → Can legislate on State List for UTs.
  • UT Legislature → Does not eliminate Parliament's legislative power.
  • Present UTs → 8.
  • UTs with Legislature → Delhi, Puducherry, Jammu and Kashmir.
  • UTs without Legislature → Andaman and Nicobar Islands, Chandigarh, DNH and Daman and Diu, Ladakh, Lakshadweep.
  • Article 239A → Puducherry model.
  • 14th Amendment → Article 239A.

Rapid Revision — TNPSC Most Expected

What is a Union Territory? → A constitutional territorial unit administered principally by the Union government.

Which Part deals with Union Territories? → Part VIII.

Which Article contains the general rule for administration of Union Territories? → Article 239.

Who administers Union Territories constitutionally? → President.

Through whom does the President administer a Union Territory? → Administrator appointed by the President.

Is an Administrator directly elected? → No.

Is an Administrator constitutionally identical to a State Governor? → No.

Can a State Governor also be appointed Administrator of a Union Territory? → Yes.

When acting as Administrator, does that Governor act on advice of the State Council of Ministers? → No.

What is the general constitutional term used for the head of a UT administration? → Administrator.

What other designations may be used? → Lieutenant Governor, Administrator or Chief Commissioner.

How many Union Territories does India presently have? → Eight.

Name them. → Andaman and Nicobar Islands, Chandigarh, Dadra and Nagar Haveli and Daman and Diu, Delhi, Jammu and Kashmir, Ladakh, Lakshadweep and Puducherry.

Which Union Territories presently have Legislatures? → Delhi, Puducherry and Jammu and Kashmir.

Does possession of a Legislature make a UT a State? → No.

Can Parliament legislate on State List matters for a UT? → Yes.

Can Parliament legislate even where a UT has its own Legislature? → Yes.

Which Article is principally associated with Puducherry's Legislature? → Article 239A.

Which Amendment inserted Article 239A? → Fourteenth Constitutional Amendment Act, 1962.

Which Act provides the principal statutory framework for Puducherry government? → Government of Union Territories Act, 1963.

Does Puducherry have a Chief Minister? → Yes.

Does Puducherry have a Lieutenant Governor? → Yes.

Can Puducherry Legislative Assembly contain nominated members? → Yes, under its statutory framework.

Which Article contains special provisions for Delhi? → Article 239AA.

Which Amendment inserted Article 239AA? → Sixty-Ninth Constitutional Amendment Act, 1991.

What is Delhi constitutionally called? → National Capital Territory of Delhi.

Is Delhi a State? → No.

Who is Delhi's Administrator? → Lieutenant Governor.

Does Delhi have a Legislative Assembly? → Yes.

Does Delhi have a Council of Ministers? → Yes.

Which three major State List subjects are excluded from Delhi Assembly's ordinary legislative power? → Public order, police and land.

Can Parliament legislate on State List matters for Delhi? → Yes.

In case of conflict, does Parliament generally retain superior legislative authority? → Yes.

Which Article deals with failure of constitutional machinery in Delhi? → Article 239AB.

Is Article 356 directly the special failure provision for Delhi? → No.

Which Article permits Ordinances by the Administrator of a UT with Legislature? → Article 239B.

Whose instructions are required before an Ordinance under Article 239B? → President.

Can an Ordinance contain something outside the territorial Legislature's competence? → No.

Which Article empowers the President to make regulations for peace, progress and good government? → Article 240.

What legal force can an Article 240 regulation have? → Force equivalent to an Act of Parliament within the applicable framework.

Which Article deals with High Courts for Union Territories? → Article 241.

Does Delhi have its own High Court? → Yes.

Which two UTs share a common High Court? → Jammu and Kashmir and Ladakh.

When was the former State of Jammu and Kashmir reorganised? → 31 October 2019.

What were the two resulting Union Territories? → Jammu and Kashmir and Ladakh.

Which one has a Legislature? → Jammu and Kashmir.

Which one has no Legislature? → Ladakh.

Which two districts comprise Ladakh in the referenced framework? → Leh and Kargil.

Does every Union Territory have Rajya Sabha representation? → No.

Which Schedule deals with Rajya Sabha seat allocation? → Fourth Schedule.

When did the modern Union Territory category emerge? → 1956 territorial reorganisation.

Which Amendment was associated with this restructuring? → Seventh Constitutional Amendment.

Which former French settlements form present Puducherry? → Puducherry, Karaikal, Mahe and Yanam.

What happened to Chandernagore? → It merged with West Bengal.

Name former Portuguese territories that entered India. → Goa, Daman, Diu, and Dadra and Nagar Haveli.

Can a Union Territory later become a State? → Yes.

Give examples. → Himachal Pradesh, Manipur, Tripura, Mizoram, Arunachal Pradesh and Goa.

Which two Union Territories were merged in 2020? → Dadra and Nagar Haveli and Daman and Diu.

What is the name of the merged UT? → Dadra and Nagar Haveli and Daman and Diu.

Which case reaffirmed that Delhi remains a Union Territory despite its special institutions? → New Delhi Municipal Council v. State of Punjab, 1997.

Which major case in 2018 dealt with Delhi's elected government and Lieutenant Governor? → Government of NCT of Delhi v. Union of India.

What principles did it emphasise? → Representative government, constitutional morality, collective responsibility and cooperative governance.

Which later case dealt with services in Delhi? → Government of NCT of Delhi v. Union of India, 2023.

Where should changing Delhi services details be updated? → Current Affairs, because the statutory and legal position can evolve.

What is the easiest Article sequence to remember? → 239 = Administration; 239A = Puducherry model; 239AA = Delhi; 239AB = Delhi constitutional failure; 239B = Ordinance; 240 = Presidential Regulations; 241 = High Courts.
